china-fort-the-heart-of-ceylon-gem-tradi:
Nestled in Beruwala, just 55 km south of Colombo, the Chinafort "Pathe" Gem Market is a living ecosystem where generations of expertise, immense trust and precious stones change hands in a uniquely vibrant open-air market.

Nestled in the historic town of Beruwala, just 55 km south of Colombo, lies the Chinafort "Pathe" Gem Market — a legendary hub that has been the pulsating heart of Sri Lanka's gem trade for centuries. This is not just a market; it is a living, breathing ecosystem where generations of expertise, immense trust, and billions of dollars in precious stones change hands in a uniquely vibrant and safe open-air environment.

Beruwala: A Historical Crossroads

Beruwala marks the site of the first Muslim settlement in Sri Lanka, established by Somali Sheikh Yusuf bin Ahmad al-Kawneyn. The town's name is believed to be derived from the Arabic "Barbareen," meaning "the place where the sail is lowered." This rich history is reflected in its unique culture, where traditional attire like the sarong is common, and the local Tamil dialect is infused with Portuguese, Arabic, and Sinhalese words — a testament to its role as a historic trading port.

Beyond gems, Beruwala is a popular tourist destination famed for its long, golden beaches and warm tropical climate, offering diving, fishing, and luxury resorts.

Chinafort: The Epicenter of the Gem Universe

While Beruwala itself has no mines, Chinafort has evolved into the largest trading market in Sri Lanka for cut and polished gemstones. For generations, this neighborhood, dominated by Sri Lankan Muslims (Ceylon Moors), has been the crucial link connecting miners from across the island to international buyers from every corner of the globe.

Why Chinafort?

The expertise here is generational. Children grow up surrounded by gems, developing an innate, almost supernatural ability to identify a stone's type, approximate weight, and value with a single glance. This laser-sharpened intuition, combined with a deep-rooted culture of trust and integrity, forms the very capital of the market. Young traders often start with little money but are entrusted with valuable stones to learn the art of the trade.

The "Pathe" Gem Street: A Global Marketplace

The famous "Pathe" street is the vibrant core of Chinafort. Here's what makes it extraordinary:

Unmatched Variety: Every type of gemstone imaginable is available — from Ceylon sapphires (blue, yellow, pink, padparadscha), rubies from Mozambique and Burma, and Mahenge spinels to Tanzanian tsavorites, Kashmir sapphires, and Brazilian tourmalines. If it exists, it can be found here.

A Safe & Open Market: Despite millions of dollars worth of gems being traded daily in the open street, it is renowned as one of the safest gem markets in the world. The community polices itself, and a person's reputation is their most valuable asset.

Accessibility: The market is open to everyone — regardless of age, nationality, or experience. On any given day, you can see 16-year-old apprentices trading alongside 75-year-old veterans.

Peak Trading Days: The market is busiest on Wednesdays and Saturdays, when international buyers flock in. The main street is closed to vehicles, creating a bustling, pedestrian-only bazaar of gems.

The Chinafort Ecosystem: From Mine to Market

The market's strength lies in its complete control over the value chain:

Sourcing: Traders have deep, trusted relationships with miners across Sri Lanka (Ratnapura, Elahera, etc.) and travel the globe to source directly from mines in Madagascar, Tanzania, Kenya, and even conflict areas like Kashmir.

Cutting & Polishing: Chinafort is a world-class center for lapidary arts. Master cutters and polishers, with skills passed down for centuries, can transform a rough stone into a brilliant masterpiece within a day. They possess proprietary knowledge on how to maximize color, brilliance, and carat weight.

Testing & Certification: Over eight certified gemological laboratories (e.g., EGL, GIC, CGL) operate within the market, providing same-day, internationally recognized reports on authenticity, treatments, and origin. This gives buyers immense confidence.

Global Reach: Chinafort traders are global citizens. They regularly attend major international jewelry shows in Hong Kong, Tucson, Bangkok, and Vicenza and have established distribution networks across the world, ensuring their stones reach the right collectors and jewelers.

A Culture of Risk and Reward

The gem trade here is not for the faint of heart. It involves:

High-Stakes Rough Trading: Evaluating and purchasing rough stones requires immense experience to avoid losses and is akin to high-stakes gambling.

Global Expeditions: Traders often spend months in remote, sometimes dangerous, mining areas across Africa and Asia, risking their health and capital to secure the finest stones.

Artistic Cutting: A wrong cut can turn a valuable rough stone into a near-worthless piece. The cutters' skill directly determines the final value.

Conclusion: More Than a Market, A Legacy

The Chinafort "Pathe" Gem Market is a phenomenon. It is a unique fusion of ancient tradition and global commerce, built on an unshakeable foundation of trust, expertise, and a fearless entrepreneurial spirit. It is not just the commercial hub of Sri Lanka's gem industry; it is a testament to the country's enduring legacy as the Rathna Deepa, and the place where the world comes to find the most beautiful treasures the earth has to offer.

For anyone in the gem and jewelry trade, a visit to the "Pathe" market is not just a business trip — it is a pilgrimage.
ceylon-sapphire-and-the-worlds-great-jew:
Ceylon gemstones are internationally celebrated, particularly for their exceptional blue sapphires and remarkable star corundum. Many of the world's largest and most famous sapphires of Sri Lankan origin now sit in royal collections and museums.

Ceylon gemstones are internationally celebrated, particularly for their exceptional blue sapphires and remarkable star corundum. Many of the world's largest and most famous sapphires of Sri Lankan origin are now part of royal collections, museums, and prestigious gemstone collections around the world.

It is believed that 17 out of 30 of the world's largest and most valuable gemstones have origins connected to Sri Lanka. Below are some of the most famous examples.

1. Giant of the Orient

The Giant of the Orient is one of the most remarkable blue sapphires associated with Sri Lanka. The enormous rough sapphire was reportedly discovered near Adam's Peak in Sri Lanka in 1902.

A major gemstone exporter of that period, O.L.M. Macan Marker & Co., purchased the rough stone when it weighed more than 600 carats. A local Sri Lankan gem cutter later cut and polished the stone, reducing its weight to approximately 466 carats.

The finished gemstone became an extraordinary cushion-cut blue sapphire with a beautiful cornflower-blue colour. At the time, it was considered one of the largest faceted blue sapphires of its kind. The stone displayed a highly saturated, intense medium-blue colour and reportedly showed an orange-red reaction under ultraviolet light. In 1902, the sapphire was valued at approximately $7,000, an extraordinary amount for that period.

The Giant of the Orient disappeared from public attention for almost a century after reportedly being sold to an anonymous American private collector in 1907. It remained largely unknown to the public until it appeared in Christie's Magnificent Jewels auction catalogue in May 2004.

Some experts later suggested that there may have been a discrepancy of approximately 20 carats in the recorded weight of the stone, possibly resulting from limitations in the measuring equipment used at the time or from an error in historical documentation.

The sapphire did not achieve a successful auction price at the Christie's event. However, it was later sold privately to an anonymous British buyer. Since then, the Giant of the Orient has not been publicly displayed again.

2. Logan Blue Sapphire

The Logan Blue Sapphire is an extraordinary gemstone weighing approximately 423 carats and is considered one of the largest and most impressive blue sapphires in the world.

The sapphire was originally discovered and cut in Sri Lanka, a country with a gemstone mining and cutting tradition extending back more than two thousand years. This magnificent cushion-cut stone displays a rich blue colour with a slight violet overtone. It is surrounded by 20 white diamonds, which further enhance the brilliance and beauty of the gemstone.

According to information provided by the Gemological Institute of America (GIA) in 1997, the Logan Sapphire's colour was naturally formed, and there was no evidence that the gemstone had undergone heat treatment. When exposed to ultraviolet radiation, the stone reportedly displays a moderate reddish-orange fluorescence.

Today, the Logan Blue Sapphire is part of the collection displayed at the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of Natural History.

3. Blue Belle of Asia

The Blue Belle of Asia is a famous and highly desirable blue sapphire originally associated with Sri Lanka.

The gemstone was reportedly discovered in a paddy field in Ratnapura in 1926 and originally weighed approximately 400 carats. The name “Belle” reflects the extraordinary beauty of this enormous blue sapphire.

The stone was once owned by Lord Nuffield of Britain and later reappeared at a Christie's auction in Geneva, Switzerland. After being recut, the gemstone weighed 395.52 carats and was mounted as part of a spectacular diamond necklace.

In 2014, the Blue Belle of Asia was sold for approximately $17.29 million, achieving what was reported as the highest price ever paid for a sapphire at auction at that time.

4. Star of Lanka

The name Star of Lanka represents both the type of gemstone and its Sri Lankan origin. This remarkable gemstone is a milky blue star sapphire featuring a clearly visible six-rayed star pattern. It weighs approximately 193 carats and was discovered in Sri Lanka during the twentieth century.

Experts have suggested that there is a significant possibility that large blue sapphires weighing more than 100 carats may originate from Sri Lanka, reflecting the country's long-standing reputation for producing exceptionally large sapphires.

The Royal Ontario Museum accurately identified and named the gemstone the Star of Lanka in order to clearly recognise its Sri Lankan origin. This differs from certain other Sri Lankan-origin gemstones displayed internationally under names associated with other countries.

The stone has a grayish-blue appearance because its milky and opaque nature partially conceals its deeper blue colour. It has been fashioned into a high-domed, oval cabochon cut, allowing its six distinctive rays to extend visibly across the surface and towards the base of the stone.

The sapphire was originally owned by Allan Kaplan, who later sold it to the Royal Ontario Museum in 1958.

5. Pride of Sri Lanka

The Pride of Sri Lanka is a gigantic deep-blue sapphire weighing approximately 856 carats.

The stone was reportedly mined in 1998 in Marapanna, around three kilometres from Ratnapura. It was discovered in mining pits associated with Ms. Leelawathi Darmadasa, who was a major shareholder in the gemstone.

According to comments made at the time, the mining region had previously produced even larger and higher-quality gemstones. However, some of those stones were allegedly sold through unofficial channels to avoid taxation. The Pride of Sri Lanka emerged during a period when tax concessions had made it easier for major gemstones to enter legitimate commercial markets.

The enormous sapphire was publicly exhibited inside a glass display case before later being moved to another location for viewing by potential buyers. It was regarded as one of the largest recorded blue sapphires discovered in Sri Lanka, and very little information about the stone has appeared publicly since that period.

Because Sri Lanka has supplied many of the world's largest sapphires, this extraordinary gemstone came to symbolise the country's pride and contribution to the international gemstone industry.

6. Grayish Blue Star of India

The Grayish Blue Star of India is one of the largest star sapphires in the world. The gemstone weighs approximately 563 carats and is considered almost flawless. One of its most remarkable characteristics is that it displays a visible star effect on both sides, an exceptionally rare feature for a sapphire of such enormous size.

Despite being called the Star of India, the gemstone is believed to have been discovered in Sri Lanka. India has not historically been known for producing sapphires of this particular size in significant numbers, which has created questions about how the stone acquired its name.

One possible explanation relates to the period of British colonial administration, when Sri Lanka was connected administratively and commercially to British-controlled India through the British East India Company. Because India was the largest and most internationally recognised territory under British administration in the region, gemstones from Sri Lanka could sometimes become associated with India in international records and trade.

The spectacular star sapphire is currently housed in the J.P. Morgan Hall at the American Museum of Natural History.

7. Naleem Alexandrite

Alexandrite is one of the world's most unusual and valuable gemstones because of its ability to display different colours under different lighting conditions. The gemstone can appear reddish under certain forms of incident light and green under natural daylight. This remarkable colour-changing characteristic makes high-quality alexandrite extremely rare and valuable.

The Naleem Alexandrite is exceptional because of its enormous size. Although some claims remain unconfirmed, it has been suggested that the stone may be one of the largest alexandrites in the world, weighing approximately 112 carats.

The gemstone was reportedly sold by the late and famous gemstone merchant Al Haj Naleem, who was associated with the gem trade in China Fort, Beruwala, Sri Lanka. The stone was named after its seller, and Al Haj Naleem was known for both his involvement in the gemstone industry and his philanthropic activities.

The Naleem Alexandrite has been valued at more than $100 million, making it potentially one of the most expensive gemstones of its type. The identity of its current owner remains unknown, and the gemstone has received little public attention since approximately 2011.

8. Rosser Reeves Star Ruby

The Rosser Reeves Star Ruby is considered one of the world's largest and finest star rubies and is associated with Sri Lanka. The gemstone is particularly remarkable because it combines several highly desirable qualities: exceptional colour, good transparency, and a clearly defined star pattern.

The stone originally weighed approximately 140 carats but was later repolished to remove surface scratches. Following this process, it became the famous 138-carat Rosser Reeves Star Ruby. The gemstone is cut as an oval cabochon with a domed surface, allowing it to display a highly precise and impressive asterism, or star effect.

Many Sri Lankan star sapphires tend to range from blue to gray because of the presence of iron. This makes the intense colour and large size of the Rosser Reeves Star Ruby particularly exceptional.

The gemstone was named after one of its former owners, Rosser Reeves, a famous American advertising executive. Reeves purchased the stone in 1950 and reportedly carried it with him during his travels because he considered it a good-luck stone.

In 1965, Rosser Reeves and his wife donated the gemstone to the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of Natural History, where it remains an important part of the collection.

9. Black Prince Ruby / Spinel

The famous Black Prince Ruby, now scientifically identified as a red spinel, is an extraordinary gemstone with a remarkable history. The gemstone weighs approximately 170 carats and is an impressive uncut red spinel.

During earlier historical periods, many transparent red gemstones were automatically assumed to be rubies. Modern gemological technology later revealed that the Black Prince Ruby was actually a red spinel.

The stone has been connected with the British Royal Family since approximately 1367 and was estimated to have a value equivalent to around £10 million in 2016. Although its exact origin has not been conclusively confirmed, it has been suggested that the gemstone may have originated from either Sri Lanka or Tajikistan.

Historical accounts also state that King Richard III wore the gemstone on his helmet during the Battle of Bosworth Field, where he died. Today, the Black Prince Spinel forms an important centrepiece of the Imperial State Crown of Great Britain and is displayed at the Tower of London.

10. British Royal Jewel

The British Royal Jewel is an exceptional 105-carat chrysoberyl cat's eye believed to have been discovered in Sri Lanka.

The gemstone gained considerable recognition after reportedly being purchased for the British Royal Family from a respected London jeweller around 1900. It is said that this extraordinary cat's eye was appreciated and treasured by four British monarchs:

King Edward VII

King George V

King Edward VIII

Queen Elizabeth II

The gemstone remains an important example of the exceptional quality of Sri Lankan chrysoberyl cat's eyes.

11. Empress Maria's Sapphire

Empress Maria's Sapphire is a magnificent oval-cut blue sapphire of Sri Lankan origin weighing approximately 260.37 carats.

The gemstone was reportedly purchased by the Russian Emperor Alexander II at the London Great Exhibition in 1862 and presented to his wife, Empress Maria Alexandrovna. The sapphire was later made the centrepiece of an elaborate brooch that also contained approximately 56 carats of diamonds.

The gemstone is considered a remarkable masterpiece because of its impressive combination of colour, cut, size, and clarity. Unlike many very large sapphires, which may display uneven colour distribution, this stone reportedly has a consistent medium-dark, richly saturated blue colour. The sapphire measures approximately 6 centimetres by 5.3 centimetres.

Following the death of the Empress in 1880, the gemstone eventually became part of the State Diamond Fund of the Russian Federation and is displayed at the museum in Gokhran, Russia. It has been recognised as one of the world's most famous and largest sapphires.

12. Bismarck Sapphire

The Bismarck Sapphire is a beautiful 98.6-carat cornflower-blue sapphire with a cushion cut. The stone is believed to have been discovered in Sri Lanka around 1920, although some sources have suggested that it may have originated in Burma and later been sold through Sri Lanka.

The sapphire displays several highly desirable characteristics, including a deep cornflower-blue colour, excellent transparency, strong clarity, and a symmetrical cut.

The gemstone was given to Countess Mona von Bismarck, a famous fashion icon of her era, by her third husband, Harrison Williams, during their honeymoon in 1926. In 1967, Mona von Bismarck donated the sapphire to the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C.

The gemstone is mounted as a pendant on a necklace featuring a platinum chain decorated with round brilliant-cut diamonds and eight smaller square-cut sapphires arranged around the setting.

13. The Eye of the Lion

The Eye of the Lion is a spectacular and priceless chrysoberyl cat's eye weighing approximately 465 carats. The enormous gemstone was discovered during the late nineteenth century in a paddy field in Pelmadulla, Ratnapura District, Sri Lanka.

The stone was originally associated with a family believed to be descended from King Rajasinghe I, who ruled Sri Lanka from 1581 to 1593. The gemstone was discovered on paddy land belonging to Iddamalgoda Kumarihamy, an aristocratic chieftain from the Sabaragamuwa Province and the Chief Custodian of the historic Saman Devale.

Iddamalgoda Kumarihamy had four daughters and reportedly presented the uncut cat's eye gemstone to the husband of her eldest daughter, who belonged to another prominent family in the region. The stone remained in its rough form for many years and was later inherited by members of the family.

Throughout history, the lion has represented strength, power, bravery, and national identity. It is famously featured on Sri Lanka's national flag. For this reason, the family named the gemstone The Eye of the Lion, representing the courage and symbolic strength of the nation.

The Smithsonian Institution reportedly expressed interest in acquiring the gemstone in 1978, after which little information about it was publicly available for nearly three decades. The stone later reappeared in 2006 at the New York laboratory of the American Gem Trade Association (AGTA) in the possession of gemstone dealer Jeffrey Bergman of Primagem in Bangkok, Thailand.

14. The Star of Artaban

The Star of Artaban is a milky blue, cabochon-cut star sapphire weighing approximately 287 carats and believed to be of Sri Lankan origin. Unlike transparent sapphires, the beauty of this gemstone is strongly influenced by its distinctive milky appearance, which reduces the transparency of the stone.

The name of the gemstone comes from the story “The Other Wise Man” by Henry van Dyke. The story follows Artaban, a wise man from Persia who intended to join the Biblical Magi on their journey to visit the newborn Jesus. Artaban purchased three valuable gemstones to offer as gifts, including a sapphire. However, he never completed his intended journey and instead used his precious possessions to help people in need.

The gemstone was reportedly purchased by a member of the Georgia Mineral Society towards the end of 1943. It was later anonymously donated by the same family to the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C.

15. Star of Bombay

The Star of Bombay is a magnificent 182-carat violet-blue star sapphire believed to have been discovered in Sri Lanka. The gemstone was given to the famous actress Mary Pickford by her husband, Douglas Fairbanks, during the 1920s. Before her death in 1979, Mary Pickford bequeathed the gemstone to the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C.

Although the gemstone carries the name of the Indian city of Bombay, it is believed to have originated in Sri Lanka. The difference between its name and its origin has created confusion among visitors and gemstone enthusiasts.

One explanation relates to the British colonial period, when the British East India Company controlled significant commercial activities throughout the region. Gemstones originating from Sri Lanka could therefore become associated with major British-controlled Indian trading centres. India has not been widely known for producing blue sapphires of this extraordinary size in the same way as Sri Lanka.

Sri Lanka, on the other hand, has been internationally recognised for centuries as a major producer of exceptionally large sapphires. Experts have argued that large blue sapphires weighing more than 100 carats have a significant possibility of being Sri Lankan in origin, making the Star of Bombay an important symbol of the country's gemstone heritage.

16. Midnight Star Sapphire

The Midnight Star Sapphire is a large and striking deep purple-violet star sapphire weighing approximately 116.75 carats. The gemstone was discovered in Sri Lanka during the nineteenth century.

The term “midnight” is sometimes associated with very dark or black star sapphires and certain deep-blue sapphires from Mogok. However, the exact reason why this particular purple-violet gemstone became known as the Midnight Star remains uncertain.

The cutting and polishing of the sapphire are believed to have taken place in Sri Lanka. Creating a high-quality star sapphire requires considerable skill and experience. Before cutting begins, the gem cutter must carefully examine the rough stone to determine whether it is capable of producing a visible and attractive star effect. The cutter responsible for the Midnight Star Sapphire successfully shaped and polished the stone to display a precise and impressive asterism.

The gemstone was believed to have been acquired by George Frederick Kunz towards the end of the nineteenth century and later sold to J.P. Morgan, who subsequently donated the Midnight Star to the American Museum of Natural History in New York during the early twentieth century.

17. Ray of Treasure

The Ray of Treasure is an exceptional 105-carat chrysoberyl cat's eye discovered in Sri Lanka. The gemstone is an excellent example of the highly desirable “milk and honey” effect, which is one of the most valued visual characteristics in high-quality cat's eye gemstones.

It possesses excellent transparency and a sharply defined silver ray, giving the stone an almost flawless appearance. The gemstone's proportions and cutting further enhance its beauty and make it a particularly desirable example of chrysoberyl cat's eye.

Its combination of exceptional transparency and a precise, visible ray is particularly impressive for a gemstone of approximately 105 carats. The Ray of Treasure is currently part of the collection of the National Gem and Jewellery Authority (NGJA) of Sri Lanka.

18. Maharani Cat's Eye

The Maharani Cat's Eye is a remarkable 58.19-carat honey-coloured chrysoberyl cat's eye discovered in Sri Lanka. The gemstone displays a sharp and clearly visible band of light known as chatoyancy.

Although chatoyancy can occur in several different gemstones, chrysoberyl is considered one of the most famous and highly valued minerals for producing this remarkable optical effect. The cat's eye phenomenon occurs when light reflects from parallel microscopic tubes, fibres, crystals, or inclusions within the gemstone.

When the stone is cut into a cabochon shape with a curved upper surface and flatter base, the reflected light becomes concentrated into a bright line resembling the eye of a cat. The Maharani Cat's Eye is considered one of the finest gemstones of its kind and is currently displayed at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C.

19. Timur Ruby / Spinel

The Timur Ruby, also known as Khiraj-i-Alam, meaning “Tribute to the World,” is a famous gemstone that was once believed to be a ruby but was later identified as a red spinel. The gemstone is an unfaceted, polished red spinel weighing approximately 361 carats.

It is believed to have been discovered in Sri Lanka and was once owned by the Mughal Emperors of India, several of whom had their names engraved directly onto the stone.

During British rule, the British took possession of the gemstone following events connected with the annexation of Punjab in 1849, together with other famous treasures such as the Koh-i-Noor diamond. The East India Company later presented the Timur Ruby/Spinel to Queen Victoria.

In 1853, the gemstone was set into a necklace created for the Queen. The necklace was later lengthened in 1911, after which the famous gemstone was rarely worn. Today, the Timur Ruby/Spinel forms part of the British Crown Jewels.

20. Star of Adam

The Star of Adam is recognised as one of the largest blue star sapphires ever discovered. The enormous gemstone weighs approximately 1,404.49 carats, or nearly 280 grams. It surpassed a previous record-holder weighing approximately 1,395 carats, which was also believed to have originated from Sri Lanka.

The Star of Adam is currently owned by an anonymous individual. The gemstone was certified by the Sri Lankan Gemological Institute as the largest blue sapphire they had ever examined and certified. It was valued at approximately $100 million, although its owner reportedly believed that it could potentially achieve around $175 million at auction.

The massive star sapphire was discovered in the Ratnapura District, one of Sri Lanka's most famous gemstone-producing regions. Its name is connected to the traditional belief that the first man, Adam, was expelled from the Garden of Eden and descended upon the mountain known as Adam's Peak, where a large footprint is traditionally preserved.

Gemstones of this enormous size are exceptionally rare. Researchers have suggested that such a gemstone may have formed deep within ancient geological structures, possibly involving granite formations dating back approximately two billion years. The gemstone may have been subjected to extreme temperatures and pressures before slowly cooling and developing over millions of years.

The discovery of the Star of Adam once again drew international attention to Sri Lanka's extraordinary reputation as one of the world's most important gemstone-producing nations.

21. Princess Diana's Engagement Ring

One of the world's most famous sapphire jewellery pieces is the engagement ring originally worn by Princess Diana. The ring features a 12-carat oval-shaped royal-blue sapphire of Sri Lankan origin, surrounded by 14 solitaire diamonds and set in 18-karat white gold.

Sri Lanka has maintained an international reputation for producing exceptional blue sapphires, and this famous royal ring became one of the best-known examples of the beauty and prestige associated with Ceylon sapphires.

The ring was presented to Princess Diana in 1981 when she became engaged to Prince Charles. It is widely reported that Diana personally selected the ring because she loved it when she first saw it.

Following Princess Diana's death, the ring was inherited by Prince William. It was later given to Catherine, Princess of Wales (Kate Middleton) as her engagement ring, and was reportedly resized to fit Catherine's finger.

A Proud Gemstone Heritage

These famous gemstones represent only a small part of Sri Lanka's extraordinary contribution to the international gem industry. From gigantic blue sapphires and rare star sapphires to exceptional chrysoberyl cat's eyes, alexandrites, rubies, and spinels, the island has produced some of the most remarkable gemstones known to the world.

Sri Lanka's centuries-old experience in gemstone mining, cutting, polishing, and trading continues to support its identity as Rathna Deepa – The Island of Jewels.

The country's gemstones are not only valuable because of their size and beauty but also because of the remarkable histories behind them. Many have travelled through royal families, museums, private collections, international auctions, and famous historical events.

Together, these extraordinary treasures continue to demonstrate why Sri Lanka remains one of the world's most respected and historically important sources of precious gemstones.
the-pathe-gem-market:
Located in the heart of China Fort, Pathe Gem Market is one of Sri Lanka's best-known destinations for gemstone trading — where generations of merchants, miners and international buyers meet.

The Heart of Beruwala’s Gem Trade

Located in the heart of China Fort, Pathe Gem Market is one of Sri Lanka’s best-known destinations for gemstone trading. The popular Pathe Gem Street brings together gem merchants, miners, dealers, collectors, and buyers from across the island, offering gemstones in an extraordinary range of varieties, sizes, qualities, and price ranges.

While much of the trading takes place along the street, the market is also home to more than 200 air-conditioned trading offices situated on both sides of the road. These offices provide a comfortable setting for buyers and sellers to examine and negotiate premium gemstones.

Despite the enormous volume of business conducted here, with gemstones worth millions of dollars changing hands, Pathe has maintained a reputation as a safe and welcoming open gem market. Its long-standing trading culture and concentration of experienced merchants have made it an important destination within Sri Lanka’s gemstone industry.

A Meeting Place for Gem Traders

Pathe is known for its open and welcoming trading environment, attracting people from different backgrounds and nationalities. Gem miners and rough-stone dealers regularly travel from Ratnapura, Balangoda, Nithigala, Elahera, and Galle to bring their stones to the market.

The trading community represents generations of experience. Some merchants began learning the gem trade as young as 16 and have continued in the industry for more than 40 to 60 years. As a result, visitors may encounter traders ranging from teenagers beginning their journey in the industry to highly experienced merchants in their seventies.

The market offers an extensive selection of gemstones, from small stones measured in points to larger stones weighing several grams. With thousands of suppliers and traders connected to the market, buyers can examine, compare, and negotiate a remarkable variety of gemstones in one location.

An International Destination for Gem Buyers

Pathe Gem Market welcomes international buyers and collectors searching for gemstones from Sri Lanka and other major gemstone-producing regions around the world. The market offers access to a broad selection of stones, including:

Sri Lankan blue, yellow, pink, violet, and Padparadscha sapphires

Burmese, Tanzanian, and Mozambique rubies

Burmese and Tanzanian blue sapphires

Kashmir blue sapphires

Kenyan Tsavorite

Spinel

Garnets

Alexandrite

Aquamarine

Topaz

Tourmaline

Emeralds

Cat’s-eye gemstones

Star sapphires

Trading Offices & Private Gem Buying

China Fort's trading network extends well beyond Sri Lanka, with merchants maintaining connections to gemstone-producing regions around the world. Rough gemstones sourced from different locations can be brought to China Fort, where they may be evaluated, cut, polished, and prepared for local or international markets.

One of the defining features of Pathe is its concentration of dedicated gem trading offices. International buyers and collectors frequently visit these establishments not only to search for a particular gemstone but also to explore the wider variety available throughout the market.

A buyer arriving in search of a Ceylon blue sapphire, for example, may also have the opportunity to examine Padparadscha sapphires, rubies, Tsavorites, Alexandrites, spinels, garnets, cat’s-eyes, and star sapphires. The market caters to a wide range of buyers, with stones ranging from smaller commercial gems to exceptional collector-quality masterpieces.

Its reputation has been built around experienced traders, competitive pricing, long-standing business relationships, and access to gemological testing facilities. More than eight recognized gem laboratories are associated with the China Fort market, allowing gemstones to be examined and certified locally.

Market Days & Trading Hours

Pathe Gem Market operates throughout the week except Friday, which is observed as the weekly holiday for the predominantly Muslim trading community. Friday is traditionally reserved for congregational prayers, family time, and rest before trading resumes.

Although business takes place throughout the week, Wednesday and Saturday are particularly active trading days, attracting international buyers from countries including China, India, Germany, Britain, the United States, and many other international markets. On these busy days, trading generally begins from around 9:00 AM and continues until approximately 3:00 PM.

During peak trading periods, the volume of merchants and visitors can become so high that vehicle access along sections of the market is restricted. Roads may be temporarily closed or traffic redirected to accommodate the large number of people walking between trading offices and conducting business.

A Remarkable Variety of Gemstones

One of the greatest attractions of Pathe is the sheer diversity of gemstones available within the market. Visitors may encounter rubies, emeralds, Alexandrites, star sapphires, cat’s-eyes, and sapphires in a wide spectrum of colours, including:

Peacock Blue

Royal Blue

Cornflower Blue

Golden Yellow

Green

Purple

Violet

Pink

White

Pinkish Orange / Padparadscha

These gemstones are available in a broad range of sizes and qualities, from smaller commercial stones to exceptional gems sought after by collectors and international jewellery houses.

For buyers interested in experiencing Sri Lanka's gemstone trade firsthand, Pathe Gem Market offers a unique opportunity to witness generations of trading knowledge, examine gemstones from multiple sources, and experience one of the country's most distinctive gem-trading environments.
heat-treatment-explained:
What heating actually does to a sapphire, which treatments the trade accepts, and which it does not.

Heat treatment has been part of the corundum trade for centuries. Applied properly, it dissolves fine silk and improves colour clarity without adding foreign material to the stone.

Accepted and unaccepted

Conventional heating is accepted worldwide when disclosed. Diffusion of colour-causing elements, glass or lead-glass filling and dyeing are different in kind: they add substance or colour from outside, and they carry very different values.

The rule that matters is disclosure. A reputable seller states treatment status on the invoice every time, without being asked.
sri-lankan-gem-heritage:
Sri Lanka, known internationally as Ceylon until 1972, has earned worldwide recognition for its remarkable wealth of gemstones and its exceptional variety of precious and semi-precious stones.

For centuries, the country's mineral-rich land has produced an extraordinary and continuing supply of high-quality gemstones. According to the ancient Sri Lankan chronicle, the Mahavamsa, the island was known as “Rathna Deepa,” a Sanskrit name meaning “The Island of Jewels.” This historic name reflects Sri Lanka's long-standing association with valuable gemstones and its rich natural resources.

Among Sri Lanka's most famous gem-producing regions is Ratnapura, commonly known as the “City of Gems” in Sinhala. The region is renowned for producing an impressive range of gemstones, many of which are considered exceptional when compared with stones found elsewhere in the world.

Since ancient times, Sri Lanka has been known for producing a wide variety of gemstones, including blue sapphires, golden yellow sapphires, pink sapphires, orange sapphires, rubies, Padparadscha sapphires, chrysoberyl cat's eyes, alexandrite, colour-changing garnets, star sapphires, garnets, zircons, tourmalines, and spinels.

A Gem History Spanning Thousands of Years

Sri Lanka's connection with gemstones extends back more than 2,500 years. Historical records and ancient chronicles contain several references to gemstones and their importance to the island's rulers and international relationships.

One ancient account refers to gem-encrusted thrones associated with a Naga king around 540 BC, providing evidence of the long history of gemstones in the region. Sri Lankan kings are also believed to have sent valuable gems and pearls to foreign rulers in order to establish diplomatic relationships and strengthen international trade.

Around 250 BC, a Sri Lankan king was reportedly said to have presented the Indian Emperor with three different varieties of gemstones and eight varieties of pearls.

References to the island's gemstones can also be found in the writings of several well-known travellers and historians. During the reign of the Roman Emperor Claudius, from AD 41 to 54, a Roman naturalist recorded information about an ambassador from Taprobane, the name by which Sri Lanka was known during that period, who spoke proudly of the island's fine gemstones.

The Greek astronomer Ptolemy, the famous traveller Marco Polo, the Arab explorer Ibn Battuta, and Robert Knox also made references to the abundance of gemstones found in Sri Lanka. Their accounts included stones such as sapphires, beryls, topaz, amethyst, and garnets, highlighting the island's reputation as an important source of valuable gems.

The Traditional Art of Gem Cutting and Polishing

Sri Lanka's gemstone industry has never been limited to mining alone. The country also has a long history of gem cutting and polishing, with these skills being practised for centuries.

Historical evidence suggests that gemstone cutting and polishing developed at an early stage in Sri Lanka's history. Gemstones discovered in the country were often cut and polished before being exported to international markets.

Over generations, Sri Lankan gem craftsmen developed extensive knowledge about different types of gemstones and the most suitable techniques for cutting each stone. This expertise became an important part of the country's gem industry and contributed to Sri Lanka's international reputation for quality gemstones and craftsmanship.

A significant portion of the traditional gem trade has historically been associated with the Ceylon Moor community, whose ancestry and long-standing connections with international trade contributed to their involvement in the industry. Their experience in trading, language skills, international travel, and commercial activities helped strengthen Sri Lanka's connections with gemstone markets around the world.

More Than Just an Island of Gems

Ceylon has long been recognised not only for its gemstones but also for its extraordinary natural beauty and abundant natural resources.

Sri Lanka provides a natural environment for a diverse range of wildlife and is home to numerous rivers that support the country's land and ecosystems. The island's tropical climate, natural landscapes, and cultural diversity have also made it an attractive destination for visitors from around the world.

Sri Lanka is home to several ethnic communities, including Sinhalese, Tamils, Muslims, and Burghers, contributing to the country's rich cultural identity.

The island is also famous for many important natural and historical attractions. According to traditional beliefs, Adam is believed to have descended upon Sri Pada, also known as Adam's Peak, where a large footprint has been preserved and respected for thousands of years.

Other important attractions include Sigiriya, the enormous natural rock fortress developed during the reign of King Kashyapa between AD 477 and 495. Sigiriya is recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and remains one of Sri Lanka's most famous historical landmarks.

The country is also known for the Sinharaja Rainforest, its beautiful tropical beaches, and numerous other natural attractions that bring visitors from different parts of the world.

Sri Lanka's Natural and Agricultural Resources

In addition to gemstones, Sri Lanka is well known for producing a variety of agricultural and commercial products. These include coconuts, rubber, tea, textiles, and spices.

Sri Lankan spices, particularly cinnamon, cardamom, and cloves, have historically played an important role in international trade.

The country's natural resources extend beyond agriculture and gemstones. Sri Lanka also possesses resources such as limestone, graphite, mineral sands, phosphates, uranium, and clay.

Its rivers have also played an important role in generating hydroelectric power, supplying electricity to industries and households throughout the country.

Early Settlements and the Arrival of Foreign Traders

Ancient stories, historical references, and legends suggest that Sri Lanka's valuable resources and natural beauty attracted people to the island from very early times.

According to traditional historical accounts, Prince Vijaya, accompanied by hundreds of followers, arrived from Southern India and established control over parts of the island after conflicts with the Yakkha inhabitants. These events are traditionally placed between approximately 543 and 505 BC. Prince Vijaya is recognised in traditional Sri Lankan history as the first king and an ancestor of the modern Sinhalese people.

As the country developed over the following centuries, traders, explorers, and voyagers increasingly travelled to Rathna Deepa to exchange valuable goods and establish commercial relationships.

Arab, Moroccan, and Somali traders visited the island at different times, particularly because of the valuable spice trade and other natural resources available in Sri Lanka.

Colonial Influence on Sri Lanka

The arrival of the Portuguese marked an important period in Sri Lankan history. Their first arrival is believed to have been largely accidental, as adverse winds and storms reportedly drove Portuguese ships towards the coast near Galle.

Although their original interest was primarily commercial, the Portuguese later became involved in the political divisions that existed within the island. Portuguese colonial rule continued from approximately 1505 until 1656.

The Dutch were later invited to assist in fighting the Portuguese. Their involvement eventually led to Dutch control over parts of Sri Lanka, which continued from 1656 until 1796.

British rule followed the Dutch period and continued until Sri Lanka gained independence in 1948.

During these colonial periods, many of Sri Lanka's natural resources, including gemstones, became increasingly connected with international trade and export markets. Gem deposits discovered throughout the island were valuable resources and contributed significantly to commercial activity.

Sri Lanka's Geological Heritage and Modern Development

Sri Lanka's unique geology has developed over millions of years, dating back to the period of the ancient supercontinent. Geological changes gradually moved the landmass from its earlier connection with regions near South-East Africa to its present strategic position in the Indian Ocean.

Today, Sri Lanka occupies an important geographical location along major maritime routes connecting the East and the West.

Following the end of the country's 25-year civil conflict in 2009, Sri Lanka experienced further development across sectors including services, industry, and agriculture.

Changes to regulations related to the mining and export of gemstones have also contributed to the continued growth of the gem industry and other sectors of the economy.

Despite centuries of change, Sri Lanka continues to maintain its historic identity as Rathna Deepa – The Island of Jewels. Its extraordinary geological resources, centuries of gemstone expertise, rich trading history, cultural diversity, and natural beauty continue to make the island one of the world's most remarkable sources of precious gemstones.
reading-rough-sapphire:
Most of a sapphire's value is decided before it is faceted. A look at how rough is evaluated in the Sri Lankan trade.

Rough gem material rarely announces itself. A water-worn pebble from the gem gravels may hide fine colour behind a frosted skin, or promise colour it cannot deliver once light passes through it properly.

Four questions

Experienced buyers work through the same considerations: how transparent is the body, where does the colour concentrate, how will the crystal shape limit the finished outline, and where do the inclusions sit relative to the future table.

The answers determine both the shape a cutter can produce and the weight loss they must accept. A stone that must be cut deep to hold colour will look different from one whose colour lies evenly through the crystal.
